claims.text: Women receive a 32.4% lower exposure rate to algorithm-driven job advertisements compared to men.
The disparity in job advertisement exposure between genders is not attributable to the gender distribution of the advertising platform's user base.
Women encounter disproportionately more shopping and entertainment advertisements in their information feeds.
Job advertisements for white-collar positions exhibit lower exposure rates for women.
Job advertisements for high-paying positions exhibit lower exposure rates for women.
Job advertisements for blue-collar occupations have higher exposure rates among women.
Job advertisements for low-paying occupations have higher exposure rates among women.
The concept of 'algorithmic crowding out' conceptualizes socioeconomic inequalities encoded in algorithms that systematically exclude women from certain job opportunities and reproduce gender orders.

evidence.description: Analysis of over 700 algorithm-driven job ads on a Chinese advertising platform showed women received a 32.4% lower exposure rate than men.
Evaluation determined the disparity is not attributable to user base gender distribution on the platform but rooted in algorithmic decision-making.
Platform findings showed women encounter disproportionately more shopping and entertainment ads alongside fewer job ads in information feeds.
Comparison of ad exposure across job categories showed ads for white-collar positions have lower exposure rates for women.
Comparison of ad exposure across job categories showed ads for high-paying positions have lower exposure rates for women.
Comparison of ad exposure across job categories showed ads for blue-collar occupations have higher exposure rates among women.
Comparison of ad exposure across job categories showed ads for low-paying occupations have higher exposure rates among women.

methodologies.name: Quantitative analysis of algorithmic job advertisement exposure
methodologies.description: Analysed over 700 algorithm-driven job advertisements on a Chinese advertising platform and compared exposure rates across genders and job types.
datasets: Chinese advertising platform ad feed dataset
conditions: Analysis of over 700 algorithm-driven job ads
Comparison of male versus female exposure rates
Categorization across white-collar vs blue-collar and high-paying vs low-paying jobs
